Some of this year’s National Book Award finalists and winners share their best advice for dealing with writer’s block, from writing by hand to reading widely.

I’ve never really had writer’s block, mostly because I refuse to acknowledge it. If something I’m writing and want to write isn’t coming, I simply tell myself it’s not ready yet, and I try to trust that it will arrive in its own time. During these times, I’ll read a lot or I’ll draft shorter pieces to keep my creative juices flowing. Middles are often where I get most stuck, after the excitement of a beginning fades, so I muddle through, writing very imperfect sentences and paragraphs until I find my way forward. I also try to use my down time from writing to reconnect with life beyond the page. Living more fully can sometimes bring the words back.
Morgan Thomas, author of Mad Eden

Writer’s block takes different forms for me, and so responding requires discernment. Generally, if I’m not eager to write there’s a good reason. It signals that I need to tend other parts of my life — explore new books or music, spend time with my family, spend time with trees, go for a walk, rest. I try to listen. But I’ve also found that I’m always reluctant to work on stories or novels when they are about 75% done. The early glamour has worn away, but I’m not yet near enough to sense the ending’s presence. I’ve learned that I have to push through here, continuing in spite of my reluctance.
Sara Nović, author of Mother Tongue

I go back to writing by hand. Usually my writer’s block manifests by me sitting at my laptop, deleting and rewriting the same sentence over and over again — which can have its merits — but if I need to generate new words, I go back to the notebook. Nothing to tweak on a blank page, so you just have to write something new. If there’s a clunky word choice or phrase I know I already hate, I just circle it as a reminder to fix it later, and I keep moving.
​Fady Joudah, author of Exhibit G: Poems, Essays, and Photographs of Gaza

I do not tackle writer’s block because I do not name it that or do not feel I have it. When I am not writing or not progressing with writing, I tend to accept it as a form of meditation, self-examination, or respite that almost always rewards me in the end. I trust that mode of silence. Much of our cultural language is based on negative emotions. Why block? Take survivor’s guilt, for example. I think it is survivor’s love. Not everything has to be a pathology that serves a market reflex.
Intan Paramaditha, author of Night of a Thousand Hells
I read. Good books spark ideas. Less good books remind me of the road I do not wish to take.
Elana K. Arnold, author of Holloway

I’ve learned that the cure for writer’s block is always this: Do more research. “Research” is an elastic word; it can mean that when I’m writing a book set in an asylum in 1946 France, I learn more about that asylum, that year, that country… but it can also mean that I spend some time thinking about how interesting it is that “asylum” has two meanings, and looking up the definitions in various dictionaries, and then reading other words that appear on those same pages, and wondering about them, and maybe re-naming one of the minor characters a derivative of one of those adjacent words… and actually, that gives me an idea for something that can happen with that minor character! Maybe she won’t be so minor after all… and I’m rushing back to my manuscript, ready to write. Research cures writer’s block because it allows my brain to unclench, to loosen from the chokehold it’s taken on my work. As I wander, unclenching, through research, I always — one hundred percent of the time — find something that clicks and reinvigorates my writing. Is this because I’ve discovered some sort of magic trick? Magic, yes; trick, no. I think it’s magical that everything is connected, and that any route I take can lead me back to my own story.​
David Levithan and Gabriel Duckels, co-authors of The Fight of Our Lives: AIDS in America
DL: I always leave myself a runway for what I want to write next.
Brenda Hillman, author of Still House in the Desert: An eco-contemplation

​I’ve never defined writer’s block. There are slower periods and periods when I write less or with less intense commitment. I adore writing, re-writing, and re-visiting old failed drafts; “fail better,” as Beckett says. I like revisiting the bone pile, the compost pile, the pile of folders or lines in notebooks, and just making the process pleasurable… so, I don’t really experience “blocks,” if the term refers to not working on writing. I like to play when I’m not following the scent of the real poem; sometimes the unreal poem and the real poem become the same thing. If writer friends or my students are being too hard or judgy on themselves, on ourselves, I always say a version of the same thing I say to myself when I’m worried: lower your expectations but not your hopes and dreams. Sometimes just getting out of bed, washing your face and writing a line in your journal is a tall order for the day, so just lower your expectation until the next day of your writing life is manageable; if writing a whole line in your journal is too much, maybe go for just one word.
​Colin Asher, author of The Midnight Special: The Secret Prison History of American Music

Being a nonfiction writer helps. I always start by revisiting my source material. If I’m working with interview transcripts, news reports, or books, I re-read them. If I’m writing about a piece of music, I put it on repeat. Often, I’m able to fill in the gaps I had been stumbling over that way. Other times, the process will make me curious about some minor point, or character, that hadn’t interested me earlier and when I investigate them I uncover new facets of my story that suggest ways forward that wouldn’t have occurred to me otherwise.

When none of that works, I go running. I’ve written some of my best lines while on long runs. And if I’m still stuck, I walk along my bookshelves, grab books at random, and flip them open to random pages. Then I read a paragraph or two before repeating the process. There’s something about dropping into someone else’s work, and thinking, that allows me to see my own writing with fresh eyes and knocks me out of whatever rut I had been lodged in so I can move forward.
Keala Kendall, author of That Which Feeds Us: A Hawaiian Gothic

When I start a project, I write a mock query letter and a like list, a running inventory of elements that make me excited about the story. I refer back to these and use them as a guiding star while drafting (though the story can always change). Whenever I get stuck, I check my list to see what I can add to the scene to spark momentum. To give you an idea of how simple this can be, here are a few items from my list for That Which Feeds Us: hiding in tall grass fields, scuttling sounds at night, luxury turning into rot in real time, and the cost of coming home.
Valeria Luiselli, author of Beginning Middle End
